transitivity: both — transitive (accelerate the car), intransitive (the truck accelerated)
gloss: To go faster, or to make a vehicle go faster.
examples: Never *accelerate* in the middle of a turn.
The van *accelerated* onto the highway.
He was *accelerating* when the light turned yellow.

gloss: To slow a vehicle down or stop it by pressing the brakes.
examples: *Brake* early when the road is wet.
She *braked* hard and the load slid forward.
The bus was *braking* the whole way down the hill.
contrast: Sounds exactly like *break* (ломать). The silent *-e* drops before *-ing*: *braking*.

transitivity: both — transitive (steer the trailer), intransitive (she steers with one hand)
gloss: To control which way a vehicle goes.
examples: A loaded truck is harder to *steer*.
He *steered* the van around the pothole.
She was *steering* while her brother read the map.

transitivity: both — transitive (park the car), intransitive (park in the back lot)
gloss: To leave a vehicle standing somewhere for a while.
examples: You cannot *park* at this curb on weekdays.
I *parked* three blocks from the restaurant.
Someone has *parked* across my driveway.

ru: сдавать назад, давать задний ход; разворачивать в обратную сторону
transitivity: both — transitive (reverse the truck), intransitive (reverse slowly)
gloss: To drive backward, or to make something go the opposite way.
examples: *Reverse* slowly until you feel the curb.
He *reversed* the trailer into the loading bay on the first try.
A camera beeps while you are *reversing*.

transitivity: both — transitive (signal a left turn), intransitive (signal before you move over)
gloss: To show which way you are about to turn, usually with a blinker.
examples: Always *signal* before changing lanes.
The driver *signaled* and pulled to the curb.
He turned without *signaling* and nearly hit us.
contrast: American spelling keeps one *l*: *signaled, signaling* (British *signalled, signalling*).

transitivity: both — transitive (honk the horn), intransitive (the taxi honked at me)
gloss: To sound a vehicle horn.
examples: Do not *honk* in a hospital zone.
The cab behind us *honked* twice.
Someone has been *honking* at that stalled van for a minute.

ru: резко сворачивать, вильнуть, свернуть в сторону
gloss: To turn suddenly to one side to avoid something.
examples: Do not *swerve* for a squirrel at highway speed.
The driver *swerved* and hit the guardrail.
A pickup was *swerving* between lanes ahead of us.

gloss: To slide out of control on a road after the tires lose grip.
examples: Worn tires *skid* on wet pavement.
The delivery van *skidded* through the intersection.
We could hear the truck *skidding* behind us.
contrast: One vowel + one consonant, so the *d* doubles: *skidded, skidding*.

transitivity: both — transitive (stall the engine), intransitive (the car stalled)
gloss: To stop running suddenly, said of an engine.
examples: Learners *stall* a stick shift on every hill.
The car *stalled* in the middle of the bridge.
It has *stalled* twice this week.

ru: ехать с ровной скоростью, двигаться крейсерским ходом
transitivity: both — transitive (cruise the coast road), intransitive (we cruised at sixty)
gloss: To travel at a steady comfortable speed.
examples: These trucks *cruise* best at sixty-five.
We *cruised* down the coast with the windows open.
The plane has been *cruising* at thirty thousand feet.

gloss: To keep moving without power, using only momentum or the slope.
examples: Take your foot off the gas and *coast* to the sign.
The truck *coasted* the last half mile on empty.
We were *coasting* downhill with the engine off.

ru: работать на холостом ходу; держать двигатель включённым
transitivity: both — transitive (do not idle your engine), intransitive (the bus idled at the curb)
gloss: To run an engine while the vehicle is not moving.
examples: Diesel engines *idle* louder than gas engines.
The bus *idled* at the curb for ten minutes.
A sign asks drivers to stop *idling* near the school.
contrast: Sounds like *idol*; the silent *-e* drops before *-ing*: *idling*.

transitivity: both — transitive (rev the engine), intransitive (the motor revved)
gloss: To make an engine turn faster and louder.
examples: Do not *rev* a cold engine.
The kid next to us *revved* his motor at every light.
Someone has been *revving* a dirt bike since six.
contrast: One vowel + one consonant, so the *v* doubles: *revved, revving*.

transitivity: both — transitive (merge the two lanes), intransitive (merge onto the freeway)
gloss: To move from one lane or road into the flow of traffic on another.
examples: Speed up before you *merge* onto the freeway.
The semi *merged* right in front of us.
Traffic slows where four lanes are *merging* into two.
contrast: You *merge* **onto** a highway and *merge* **with** traffic.

transitivity: both — transitive (yield the right of way), intransitive (yield to oncoming traffic)
gloss: To let other traffic go first.
examples: Drivers turning left must *yield* to oncoming cars.
He never *yielded* and the two cars nearly touched.
The truck was *yielding* to a school bus.
contrast: In driving it takes **to**: *yield to pedestrians*. The American sign says YIELD where British signs say GIVE WAY.

transitivity: both — transitive (tailgate the car ahead), intransitive (stop tailgating)
gloss: To drive too close behind another vehicle.
examples: Please do not *tailgate* on an icy road.
A pickup *tailgated* us for ten miles.
He rear-ended her because he was *tailgating*.

gloss: To change direction suddenly, usually to one side.
examples: The road *veers* left after the bridge.
The van *veered* into the shoulder.
A sleepy driver was *veering* toward the median.

transitivity: both — transitive (slow the truck), intransitive (traffic slowed)
gloss: To move more slowly, or to make something move more slowly.
examples: Rain will *slow* the whole delivery route.
Traffic *slowed* to a crawl near the tunnel.
The train was *slowing* as it entered the yard.

transitivity: both — transitive (halt the convoy), intransitive (the train halted)
gloss: To stop moving, or to bring something to a stop.
examples: A flagger can *halt* traffic in both directions.
The freight train *halted* just short of the crossing.
Shipments have been *halted* until the storm passes.

transitivity: both — transitive (stop the car), intransitive (stop at the sign)
gloss: To come to rest, or to bring a vehicle to rest.
examples: You must *stop* completely at a red light.
She *stopped* for gas outside Denver.
The bus is *stopping* at every corner today.
contrast: One vowel + one consonant, so the *p* doubles: *stopped, stopping*.

transitivity: both — transitive (start the engine), intransitive (the truck would not start)
gloss: To make an engine begin to run, or to begin to run.
examples: *Start* the car and let it warm up.
The van *started* on the third try.
It has not *started* once since the cold snap.

transitivity: both — transitive (turn the wheel), intransitive (turn at the light)
gloss: To change the direction you are driving in.
examples: *Turn* right at the second light.
We *turned* onto a gravel road by mistake.
The truck was *turning* wide and blocked both lanes.

transitivity: both — transitive (navigate the canal), intransitive (I drive, she navigates)
gloss: To find and follow the right route.
examples: I drive and my sister *navigates*.
We *navigated* the whole detour without a phone.
He has *navigated* these back roads for years.

transitivity: both — transitive (maneuver the trailer), intransitive (maneuver around the crates)
gloss: To move a vehicle carefully into or through a tight place.
examples: It takes practice to *maneuver* a long trailer.
She *maneuvered* the forklift between two pallets.
He was *maneuvering* out of the space when the mirror caught.
contrast: American spelling *maneuver*; British *manoeuvre*.

transitivity: both — transitive (shift gears), intransitive (shift into third)
gloss: To change gears in a vehicle.
examples: You have to *shift* down before the hill.
He *shifted* into reverse and backed out.
She was still *shifting* when the light changed.

transitivity: both — transitive (race the delivery van), intransitive (they raced down the block)
gloss: To go very fast, often to beat someone or something.
examples: Kids *race* their bikes down that hill every evening.
He *raced* to the airport and still missed the flight.
Two cars were *racing* on an empty stretch of highway.

transitivity: both — transitive (pass a slow truck), intransitive (no passing on a curve)
gloss: To go by another vehicle that is moving more slowly.
examples: Do not *pass* on a double yellow line.
We *passed* three trucks on the grade.
A car was *passing* us as the lane ended.
contrast: The past *passed* sounds exactly like *past*: *we passed the exit* but *we drove past the exit*.

gloss: To move slowly sideways out of your lane or course.
examples: Tired drivers *drift* toward the shoulder.
The car *drifted* over the center line.
The ferry was *drifting* away from the dock.

gloss: To move very slowly, said of traffic or a vehicle.
examples: Cars *crawl* through that tunnel every morning.
We *crawled* twelve miles in an hour.
Traffic has been *crawling* since the accident.

transitivity: both — transitive (the parade jammed the streets), intransitive (the seatbelt jammed)
gloss: To block something completely, or to get stuck and stop working.
examples: A single stalled truck can *jam* the whole bridge.
The belt *jammed* and would not pull out.
Fans have *jammed* every road near the stadium.
contrast: One vowel + one consonant, so the *m* doubles: *jammed, jamming*.

gloss: To stand in the way so that traffic cannot get through.
examples: Please do not *block* the loading dock.
A delivery van *blocked* our driveway all morning.
The left lane is *blocked* by a disabled bus.

ru: ехать в объезд, объезжать, делать крюк
transitivity: both — transitive (they detoured the traffic), intransitive (we detoured through town)
gloss: To take a different route because the usual one is closed.
examples: We can *detour* around the closed bridge.
The truck *detoured* through two small towns.
Traffic has been *detoured* onto a county road.

gloss: To pull a vehicle or trailer behind another one.
examples: They will *tow* your car if you park here.
A pickup *towed* us to the shop.
His truck was *towing* a boat up the grade.
contrast: /toʊ/ rhymes with *go* and sounds exactly like *toe*.

gloss: To take a vehicle away and hold it legally until fines are paid.
examples: The city can *impound* a car with unpaid tickets.
Police *impounded* the truck at the scene.
Her van has been *impounded* since Friday.

gloss: To give a driver an official notice of a fine.
examples: They *ticket* every car in this lot after six.
An officer *ticketed* me for a broken taillight.
He has been *ticketed* twice this month.
contrast: Stress falls on the first syllable, so the *t* does not double: *ticketed, ticketing*.

transitivity: both — transitive (refuel the plane), intransitive (we refueled in Reno)
gloss: To put more fuel into a vehicle.
examples: We can *refuel* at the next truck stop.
The crew *refueled* the plane in twenty minutes.
The ferry was *refueling* when we boarded.
contrast: American spelling keeps one *l*: *refueled, refueling* (British *refuelled, refuelling*).

transitivity: both — transitive (charge the car), intransitive (it charges overnight)
gloss: To put electric power into a battery or an electric vehicle.
examples: You can *charge* the car at any station on this route.
I *charged* it overnight in the garage.
The van has been *charging* for two hours.

transitivity: both — transitive (inflate the tires), intransitive (the airbag inflates instantly)
gloss: To fill something with air until it is firm.
examples: *Inflate* the tires to thirty-five pounds.
He *inflated* the spare before the trip.
The airbag had already *inflated* when help arrived.

transitivity: both — transitive (rotate the tires), intransitive (the wheel rotates freely)
gloss: To turn something around, or to move tires to different positions so they wear evenly.
examples: *Rotate* the tires every five thousand miles.
The shop *rotated* them and checked the brakes.
Nobody has *rotated* these tires in years.

gloss: To fix something that is broken or damaged.
examples: It will cost more to *repair* the bumper than to replace it.
They *repaired* the radiator in one afternoon.
The crew is *repairing* the guardrail at mile twelve.

gloss: To check and maintain a vehicle or machine so it keeps working.
examples: You should *service* the van before a long haul.
The dealer *serviced* my car last spring.
Two trucks are being *serviced* this week.

gloss: To look at something carefully to see whether it is safe or correct.
examples: The state will *inspect* the truck every year.
A mechanic *inspected* the brakes before the trip.
The cargo is being *inspected* at the border.

gloss: To put a new part in place of an old or broken one.
examples: We need to *replace* both front tires.
They *replaced* the windshield in an hour.
The battery has already been *replaced* once.

gloss: To put a part or device in place so that it can be used.
examples: They can *install* a tow hitch while you wait.
The shop *installed* a new car seat for us.
A dash camera has been *installed* in every van.
contrast: Two *l*s in American English: *install, installed, installing*.

gloss: To keep something in good condition, or to keep something at the same level.
examples: *Maintain* a safe distance from the truck ahead.
He *maintained* the same speed for two hundred miles.
The fleet is well *maintained*.

transitivity: both — transitive (adjust the mirrors), intransitive (your eyes adjust to the dark)
gloss: To move something slightly so that it is in the right position.
examples: *Adjust* your mirrors before you pull out.
She *adjusted* the seat and the headrest.
He was *adjusting* the straps when the truck moved.

transitivity: both — transitive (buckle the child in), intransitive (buckle up before we go)
gloss: To fasten a belt or strap with a buckle.
examples: *Buckle* your seat belt before I start the car.
She *buckled* the toddler into his seat.
He drove off without *buckling*.

gloss: To close or attach something firmly.
examples: Please *fasten* your seat belt for landing.
He *fastened* the straps over the load.
The crate was *fastened* to the pallet with steel bands.
contrast: The *t* is silent: /ˈfæsən/, like *listen* and *castle*.

gloss: To hold something in place with a strap or belt.
examples: *Strap* the ladder to the roof rack.
They *strapped* the mattress onto the trailer.
The bikes are *strapped* down for the drive.
contrast: One vowel + one consonant, so the *p* doubles: *strapped, strapping*.

gloss: To fix something firmly so that it cannot move or fall.
examples: *Secure* the load before you leave the yard.
The driver *secured* the pallets with netting.
Everything has been *secured* for the ferry crossing.

transitivity: both — transitive (tighten the straps), intransitive (the cable tightened)
gloss: To make something firmer or less loose.
examples: *Tighten* the lug nuts in a star pattern.
He *tightened* the straps at every rest stop.
The rope was *tightening* as the truck pulled away.

transitivity: both — transitive (lock the trailer), intransitive (the doors lock automatically)
gloss: To close something with a key or a latch so it cannot be opened.
examples: *Lock* the cargo doors before you leave.
I *locked* my keys in the car again.
The wheels had *locked* on the ice.

gloss: To open a lock so that something can be opened.
examples: The app can *unlock* the car from your phone.
He *unlocked* the back of the truck for the inspector.
The bike was left *unlocked* at the station.

transitivity: both — transitive (he crashed his father's car), intransitive (two cars crashed)
gloss: To hit something violently while moving.
examples: Drive slower or you will *crash*.
A delivery truck *crashed* into the median.
Nobody was hurt when the bus *crashed*.
contrast: You *crash* **into** something: *crashed into a pole*.

gloss: To hit another moving thing hard.
examples: Two trains almost *collide* at that junction every year.
The van *collided* with a parked car.
The ships were *colliding* before either could turn.
contrast: Takes **with**: *collided with a truck*, not *collided a truck*.

gloss: To damage a vehicle so badly that it is destroyed.
examples: One bad night can *wreck* a new car.
He *wrecked* the truck on a logging road.
The van was *wrecked* but the driver walked away.
contrast: The *w* is silent: /rɛk/, the same sound as in *wrench* and *write*.

gloss: To press a hollow mark into metal by hitting it.
examples: A shopping cart can *dent* a door.
Someone *dented* my fender in the parking garage.
The hood is *dented* on the driver side.

transitivity: both — transitive (scrape the bumper), intransitive (the trailer scraped along the wall)
gloss: To rub hard against something and damage the surface.
examples: Low curbs *scrape* the front bumper.
I *scraped* the side of the van in a narrow alley.
The muffler was *scraping* the whole way home.

transitivity: both — transitive (bump the car ahead), intransitive (we bumped along the dirt road)
gloss: To knock lightly against something.
examples: Do not *bump* the car in front while parking.
She *bumped* the mirror on the garage door.
The truck was *bumping* over the rail crossing.
contrast: You *bump* **into** something you did not mean to hit.

gloss: To harm something so that it works less well or looks worse.
examples: Potholes *damage* the suspension.
The hail *damaged* every car in the lot.
Two crates arrived *damaged*.

ru: разбить машину полностью (так, что ремонт дороже её стоимости)
gloss: To wreck a vehicle so badly that it is worth less than the repair.
examples: One bad slide can *total* a car.
He *totaled* his truck on the interstate.
The insurance company has *totaled* it.
contrast: American spelling keeps one *l*: *totaled, totaling* (British *totalled*).

transitivity: both — transitive (the wind flipped the trailer), intransitive (the truck flipped)
gloss: To turn over completely.
examples: A high trailer can *flip* in a crosswind.
The pickup *flipped* twice and landed upright.
Wind was *flipping* empty carts across the lot.
contrast: One vowel + one consonant, so the *p* doubles: *flipped, flipping*.

transitivity: both — transitive (load the truck), intransitive (we load at six)
gloss: To put goods into or onto a vehicle.
examples: We *load* the vans before sunrise.
They *loaded* forty boxes in half an hour.
The trailer is being *loaded* at dock three.
contrast: You *load* boxes **onto** a truck, or *load* a truck **with** boxes.

transitivity: both — transitive (unload the van), intransitive (they unload at the side door)
gloss: To take goods off or out of a vehicle.
examples: Two people can *unload* this truck in an hour.
We *unloaded* the furniture in the rain.
The crew has already *unloaded* half the container.

gloss: To carry a heavy load, usually by truck.
examples: That trailer can *haul* three tons.
He *hauled* gravel all summer.
The truck was *hauling* lumber to the coast.
contrast: Sounds exactly like *hall* (коридор, зал).

gloss: To raise something to a higher position.
examples: Two of us can *lift* the crate together.
The forklift *lifted* the pallet onto the truck.
He hurt his back *lifting* boxes all day.

gloss: To move something down to a lower position.
examples: *Lower* the ramp before you roll the cart down.
They *lowered* the engine into the boat with a crane.
The tailgate was *lowered* for loading.

ru: складывать штабелем, укладывать друг на друга
gloss: To put things one on top of another in a neat pile.
examples: Do not *stack* these boxes more than four high.
They *stacked* the pallets against the far wall.
Crates were *stacked* to the ceiling of the container.

gloss: To put something away neatly in a space made for it.
examples: Please *stow* your bag under the seat.
He *stowed* the straps in the side box.
All the gear has been *stowed* below deck.
contrast: Rhymes with *go*, not with *cow*: /stoʊ/.

transitivity: both — transitive (pack the boxes), intransitive (we packed all night)
gloss: To put things into a box, bag, or vehicle for carrying.
examples: *Pack* the fragile items last.
She *packed* the whole kitchen in two days.
They were *packing* the trailer when the rain started.
contrast: One vowel + one final consonant sound, but the *k* is not doubled: *packed, packing*.

transitivity: both — transitive (unpack the boxes), intransitive (we unpacked for hours)
gloss: To take things out of a box, bag, or vehicle.
examples: We can *unpack* the truck tomorrow.
He *unpacked* the shipment and checked every item.
She has been *unpacking* since the movers left.

gloss: To close a package or container so that nothing gets in or out.
examples: *Seal* the box with packing tape, not masking tape.
They *sealed* the container and attached a numbered tag.
Every carton arrived *sealed*.

gloss: To put a label on something showing what it is or where it goes.
examples: *Label* every box with the room it belongs in.
She *labeled* the crates FRAGILE in red marker.
The pallet was not *labeled* and went to the wrong city.
contrast: American spelling keeps one *l*: *labeled, labeling* (British *labelled, labelling*).

transitivity: both — transitive (weigh the package), intransitive (the crate weighs fifty pounds)
gloss: To have a certain weight, or to measure how heavy something is.
examples: Loaded trucks must *weigh* in at the station.
The clerk *weighed* my package and quoted the postage.
They are *weighing* the trailer before it crosses.
contrast: The *gh* is silent: /weɪ/, exactly like *way*.

transitivity: both — transitive (transfer the cargo), intransitive (transfer at the next station)
gloss: To move from one vehicle or line to another, or to move goods from one to another.
examples: You *transfer* to the blue line downtown.
They *transferred* the containers to a smaller ship.
We were *transferring* our bags when the bus pulled out.
contrast: Stress on the second syllable, so the *r* doubles: *transferred, transferring*.

ru: обращаться (с грузом), управляться; вести себя (о машине)
transitivity: both — transitive (handle the crates), intransitive (the van handles well in snow)
gloss: To touch and move something, or to behave in a certain way when driven.
examples: *Handle* the glass panels with both hands.
The loaded truck *handled* badly in the wind.
This box has been *handled* roughly.

gloss: To take something from one place to another.
examples: This ferry can *carry* eighty cars.
The train *carried* grain to the coast.
He was *carrying* two boxes up the ramp.
contrast: Consonant + *-y* changes: *carry → carries, carried*, but *carrying* keeps the *y*.

gloss: To attach a trailer to a vehicle that will pull it.
examples: *Hitch* the trailer and check the lights.
He *hitched* the boat to his pickup.
The camper was *hitched* to an old van.
contrast: Ends in *-ch*, so the third person adds *-es*: *hitches*.

transitivity: both — transitive (deliver the package), intransitive (we deliver on Sundays)
gloss: To bring goods to the place or person they are going to.
examples: They *deliver* anywhere in the county.
The driver *delivered* the couch on Saturday.
Your order has been *delivered* to the front desk.
contrast: You *deliver* something **to** a person or address.

transitivity: both — transitive (ship the order), intransitive (we ship worldwide)
gloss: To send goods somewhere by truck, plane, or boat.
examples: We can *ship* it overnight for extra.
They *shipped* the parts from Ohio.
Your order is *shipping* today.
contrast: One vowel + one consonant, so the *p* doubles: *shipped, shipping*.

gloss: To send a letter or package through the postal service.
examples: I will *mail* the documents tomorrow.
She *mailed* the package from the post office.
The check was *mailed* on Friday.
contrast: American English says *mail a letter*; British English says *post a letter*.

gloss: To send a vehicle, person, or shipment out to a destination.
examples: They *dispatch* trucks every two hours.
The office *dispatched* a tow truck within minutes.
Two vans have been *dispatched* to the warehouse.

gloss: To send something on to another address.
examples: The post office will *forward* your mail for a year.
They *forwarded* the package to my new address.
Everything is being *forwarded* to the Denver office.
contrast: You *forward* something **to** an address.

ru: направлять, прокладывать маршрут, пускать по маршруту
gloss: To send something or someone along a particular way.
examples: They *route* all freight through Memphis.
The dispatcher *routed* us around the closure.
Traffic is being *routed* onto the frontage road.
contrast: Americans say /ruːt/ or /raʊt/; both are common. The silent *-e* drops: *routing*.

gloss: To follow where a package or vehicle is at each stage.
examples: You can *track* the shipment with this number.
I *tracked* the package all the way from Texas.
The fleet is *tracked* by GPS.

gloss: To read a barcode or label with a machine.
examples: The driver will *scan* the label at pickup.
They *scanned* every box onto the truck.
Your parcel was last *scanned* in Phoenix.
contrast: One vowel + one consonant, so the *n* doubles: *scanned, scanning*.

transitivity: both — transitive (sign the form), intransitive (someone has to sign for it)
gloss: To write your name to show that you received or agreed to something.
examples: Someone has to *sign* for this delivery.
My neighbor *signed* for the package.
The driver is *signing* the manifest now.
contrast: The *g* is silent: /saɪn/. You *sign* **for** a delivery.

gloss: To get something that is sent or given to you.
examples: We *receive* shipments every Tuesday.
She *received* the parcel two days late.
The warehouse has *received* forty pallets this morning.
contrast: *ei* after *c*: *receive*, not *recieve*.

transitivity: both — transitive (return the rental car), intransitive (they returned on Sunday)
gloss: To give or send something back, or to come back.
examples: You must *return* the rental with a full tank.
He *returned* the trailer a day late.
The shipment is being *returned* to the sender.

gloss: To arrange for something to happen at a particular time.
examples: Let us *schedule* the pickup for Monday.
They *scheduled* the delivery between two and four.
The flight is *scheduled* to depart at six.
contrast: American /ˈskɛdʒuːl/ begins with *sk-*; British /ˈʃɛdjuːl/ begins with *sh-*.

gloss: To say officially that something is correct or arranged.
examples: Please *confirm* the delivery address.
They *confirmed* our seats on the later train.
Your reservation has been *confirmed*.

transitivity: both — transitive (book a flight), intransitive (book early for the holidays)
gloss: To arrange in advance to have a seat, room, or vehicle.
examples: *Book* the rental car before prices go up.
We *booked* two seats on the night train.
The ferry is fully *booked* for the weekend.

gloss: To arrange for something to be kept for you.
examples: You can *reserve* a parking spot online.
I *reserved* a van for the move.
These two spaces are *reserved* for loading.

gloss: To send goods to another country to be sold.
examples: They *export* citrus to Canada and Japan.
The company *exported* forty containers last year.
Most of this grain is *exported* by rail and ship.
contrast: The verb is stressed on the second syllable (ik-SPORT); the noun on the first (EK-sport).

gloss: To bring goods into a country from abroad.
examples: They *import* parts from three countries.
We *imported* the whole shipment through Long Beach.
These bikes are *imported* from Taiwan.
contrast: The verb is stressed on the second syllable (im-PORT); the noun on the first (IM-port).

gloss: To send goods out to the places or people that will get them.
examples: One warehouse can *distribute* to six states.
They *distributed* the relief supplies by truck.
The weight must be evenly *distributed* in the trailer.

gloss: To pay a company so that it will cover the cost if something is lost or damaged.
examples: You can *insure* the package for its full value.
He *insured* the truck before the first haul.
The cargo was *insured* against water damage.
contrast: *Insure* (страховать) is not *ensure* (обеспечить, гарантировать).

gloss: To tell customs officially what goods you are carrying.
examples: You must *declare* anything worth over eight hundred dollars.
She *declared* two bottles of wine at the border.
The shipment was *declared* as machine parts.

ru: ездить на работу и обратно, добираться до работы
gloss: To travel regularly between home and work.
examples: Thousands *commute* into the city by train.
He *commuted* two hours each way for a year.
She has been *commuting* by bike since spring.

transitivity: both — transitive (travel the whole coast), intransitive (we travel by train)
gloss: To go from one place to another, especially a long way.
examples: We *travel* by train whenever we can.
They *traveled* eight hundred miles in two days.
The shipment has *traveled* through four states.
contrast: American spelling keeps one *l*: *traveled, traveling, traveler* (British *travelled, travelling, traveller*).

ru: садиться (в самолёт, поезд, автобус), совершать посадку
transitivity: both — transitive (board the plane), intransitive (we board at gate nine)
gloss: To get onto a plane, train, bus, or ship.
examples: Passengers with children *board* first.
We *boarded* the ferry at seven.
They are *boarding* rows twenty and up.

gloss: To leave, said especially of trains, planes, and ships.
examples: The bus *departs* from the lower level.
Our flight *departed* forty minutes late.
Trains are *departing* on time despite the snow.
contrast: *Depart* is the word on timetables; in speech Americans usually say *leave*.

transitivity: both — transitive (land the plane), intransitive (we landed at noon)
gloss: To come down onto the ground from the air, or to bring a plane down.
examples: Small planes can *land* on that strip.
We *landed* in Chicago an hour late.
The plane was *landing* as the storm arrived.

gloss: To move slowly along the ground, said of an airplane.
examples: Planes *taxi* to the far end of the runway.
We *taxied* for twenty minutes before takeoff.
The jet was still *taxiing* when the crew stood up.
contrast: Odd forms: *taxis, taxied*, but *taxiing* keeps both *i*s.

transitivity: both — transitive (dock the boat), intransitive (the ferry docks at noon)
gloss: To bring a boat or ship alongside a dock, or to arrive there.
examples: The ferry *docks* at noon.
The freighter *docked* in Oakland overnight.
A cruise ship was *docking* as we drove past.

ru: плыть, идти под парусом; отплывать, отходить
transitivity: both — transitive (sail the boat home), intransitive (we sail at dawn)
gloss: To travel on water, or to leave port.
examples: The ship *sails* at six in the morning.
They *sailed* from Seattle to Alaska.
We were *sailing* into a headwind all afternoon.
contrast: Sounds exactly like *sale* (распродажа).

gloss: To carry people or goods across water, or back and forth over a short route.
examples: Two boats *ferry* workers to the island each morning.
A barge *ferried* the trucks across the river.
Vans were *ferrying* passengers between the terminals.
contrast: Consonant + *-y* changes: *ferries, ferried*, but *ferrying* keeps the *y*.

transitivity: both — transitive (shuttle the guests to the airport), intransitive (buses shuttle between terminals)
gloss: To travel back and forth between two places, or to carry people that way.
examples: Vans *shuttle* between the lot and the terminal.
The hotel *shuttled* us to the airport at five.
A small bus was *shuttling* fans to the stadium.

gloss: To call to a taxi or driver to stop for you.
examples: It is hard to *hail* a cab in the rain.
He *hailed* a taxi outside the station.
She was *hailing* a cab with one arm and holding her bag with the other.

ru: ездить вместе на одной машине (по очереди)
gloss: To share one car with other people for a regular trip.
examples: Three of us *carpool* to the plant.
They *carpooled* all through college.
We have been *carpooling* since gas went up.

transitivity: both — transitive (pedal the bike uphill), intransitive (she pedaled hard)
gloss: To push the pedals of a bicycle to make it move.
examples: You have to *pedal* hard on that hill.
He *pedaled* ten miles to work.
She was *pedaling* along the shoulder of the highway.
contrast: American spelling keeps one *l*: *pedaled, pedaling*. Sounds like *peddle* (торговать вразнос).

gloss: To pay to use a vehicle for a period of time.
examples: We can *rent* a van for the weekend.
They *rented* a car at the airport.
He has *rented* the same truck twice this month.
contrast: Americans *rent a car*; the British *hire a car*.

gloss: To say that something arranged will not happen.
examples: They may *cancel* the afternoon route.
The airline *canceled* our flight twice.
Three deliveries have been *canceled* because of the storm.
contrast: American spelling keeps one *l* in *canceled, canceling*, but the noun always has two: *cancellation*.

gloss: To make something happen later than planned.
examples: Fog can *delay* every flight on the board.
An accident *delayed* us by two hours.
The shipment has been *delayed* at customs.
contrast: Vowel + *-y*, so the *y* stays: *delayed, delaying* (compare *carry → carried*).

gloss: To move people or goods from one place to another.
examples: Tankers *transport* fuel to the depot.
They *transported* the horses in a padded trailer.
Cars are *transported* on double-deck trucks.
contrast: The verb is stressed on the second syllable (trans-PORT); the noun on the first (TRANS-port).

transitivity: both — transitive (flash your headlights), intransitive (the turn signal flashes)
gloss: To make a light shine briefly, often as a signal to another driver.
examples: Drivers *flash* their lights to warn you about the radar.
The truck ahead *flashed* its lights and pulled over.
A tow truck was *flashing* its yellow lights on the shoulder.

transitivity: both — transitive (roll the cart down the ramp), intransitive (the truck rolled forward)
gloss: To move along on wheels, or to push something along on wheels.
examples: Do not let the cart *roll* off the ramp.
The car *rolled* back a foot before he hit the brake.
They were *rolling* pallets into the trailer two at a time.

transitivity: both — transitive (connect the trailer brakes), intransitive (we connect in Dallas)
gloss: To change to another flight, train, or bus that continues your trip.
examples: We *connect* in Dallas with an hour to spare.
They *connected* through Atlanta both ways.
He missed his *connecting* flight by ten minutes.
contrast: You *connect* **to** or **with** a flight, and *connect* **in** a city.

gloss: To hand a bag over to be carried in the hold, or to look at something to make sure it is right.
examples: You can *check* two bags on this airline.
He *checked* the oil before the drive.
Our luggage was *checked* all the way to Rome.

transitivity: both — transitive (exit the highway), intransitive (exit at the next ramp)
gloss: To leave a road, building, or vehicle.
examples: *Exit* at the next ramp and turn left.
We *exited* the highway one exit too soon.
Trucks were *exiting* single file behind the police car.
contrast: Stress is on the first syllable, so the *t* does not double: *exited, exiting*.
